title: Initial Thoughts on Vagrantsong (WARNING! Incoming Rambling Thoughts!)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bQaZqs74i2Y

Daniel (@dungeondive) shares early, self-confessedly rambling impressions of *Vagrantsong*, the cooperative, story-driven ghost battler from the makers of Malifaux, after two plays of the first scenario. His pre-order took a second printing to arrive. You play vagrants who hop aboard the Silver Ferryman, a ghost train, and face the haints haunting it. The aim is to restore their humanity rather than destroy them, and he calls that a pleasant twist on a common trope.

His biggest praise goes to economy. Everything in the box fits on his small table at once, and acrylic standees replace miniatures (which, along with the smaller box, is why he backed this over Townsfolk Tussle). Tokens are reused in different roles from scenario to scenario. The bindle bag of rummage tokens (nails, candles, salt, a rabbit's foot) provides your items and also drives the haint's turn. Skills double as hit-point banks: lose ten humanity and a skill flips wounded, and lose enough and you turn into a ghost. If a scenario ends while you're still a ghost, you lose a skill for good.

There's a light legacy layer (85 unlockable skills, tiered junk, rituals as side quests, story cards with blind choices), short paragraph reads and a fail-forward camp phase. His gripe is the rulebook, which has no index and never explains how to set up the bindle bag. His verdict is that it feels like a sprawling epic without the sprawl.

----

Do you prefer games that stretch a small set of components across many roles, or does reusing tokens make things harder to follow?
